caption:
Sam Altman has said the world may have to accept "some bad things happening," including major hacks, in return for AI's benefits.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang disagrees: he told Fortune he is willing to accept no cybersecurity incidents at all.
He says AI agents should be sealed in secure containers.

Who is right, Huang or Altman?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Fortune · Photo: Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images

slides.headline: Sam Altman says we must accept some AI hacks. Jensen Huang says *zero*

slides.heading: Altman's *trade-off*
paras: Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world may have to accept "some bad things happening" for AI's benefits, including major hacks, misuse and scams.
He argued people would do "orders of magnitude" more good than harm with the technology.

slides.heading: Huang's *zero tolerance*
paras: In an interview with Fortune in London, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang pushed back: "I'm willing to accept no incidents of cybersecurity. We should not accept any of them."
"We should do everything we can to avoid them," he added.

slides.heading: Put agents *in a box*
paras: Huang said the AI agent incidents so far could have been avoided with stronger containment and monitoring.
He compared it to early web browsers learning to isolate websites, and said agents should be sealed in secure containers.

slides.heading: A message for *doomers*
paras: Huang also said AI is "completely in our control."

paras.t: If people believe AI will end human civilization, he said, "they really ought to stop working on it."

slides.hook: The two most powerful men in AI disagree on how safe it must be. Follow to see who wins.
